title: No one is immune to misinformation: An investigation of misinformation sharing by subscribers to a fact-checking newsletter
screen_reason: Online survey of 1,397 Australian subscribers to the RMIT ABC Fact Check CoronaCheck newsletter (December 2020). Table 3 reports two self-reported sharing shares against the full sample: 339 (24.3%) answered yes to 'Have you shared possible misinformation?' and 440 (31.4%) to 'Have you shared information that you later discovered was false?'. Those are shares of respondents reporting having shared misinformation = RECALL (sharing). The paper's other content (belief in science, conspiracy mentality, vaccine acceptance, regression predictors) is out of scope.

estimates.platform: self-reported sharing (platform not specified in the item; respondents' main news platforms were online newspapers 30.3%, news aggregators 24.8%, television 16.8%, social media feed 8.7%)
estimates.date: December 2020 (recruitment calls in the CoronaCheck newsletters of 11 and 18 December 2020)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who reported having shared possible misinformation, i.e. information whose truth value was unknown to them at the time of sharing
estimates.value_raw: Have you shared possible misinformation? Yes 339 (24.3%); No 1052 (75.4%); Did not answer 6 (0.4%)
estimates.denominator: 1,397 Australian subscribers to the CoronaCheck fact-checking newsletter who completed the online Qualtrics survey (1,576 took part; 29 duplicates and 150 with >20% missing data excluded)
estimates.definition: Respondent answered 'Yes' to "whether they have shared possible misinformation, i.e. information for which the truth value was not known to them at the time of sharing" (Yes/No item, no time window given).
estimates.misinfo_def: "possible misinformation" = "information whose truth value is unknown to the sharer at the time of sharing" (also described as "unverified content"); the paper distinguishes sharing false information believed true, sharing information that could be either true or false, and sharing information believed false.
estimates.source_quote: Have you shared possible misinformation? Yes 339 24.3 No 1052 75.4 Did not answer 6 0.4
estimates.page_loc: Table 3, p. 7; restated in Results 3.3 ("Of the 1397 participants, 339 (24%) indicated that they had shared unverified content") and in the Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Entirely self-reported on an anonymous Qualtrics survey; no verification of what respondents actually shared and no external ground truth. The respondent's own uncertainty at the time of sharing is the criterion, so nothing is checked against fact-checks.
estimates.moderator_quote: Participants were recruited via a call for participants published in the two editions of the CoronaCheck newsletter released on the 11th and 18th of December 2020. In total, 1576 Australian participants took part in our study by completing our online survey. ... The final sample therefore consisted of 1397 participants.
estimates.notes: 339/1397 = 24.3%, matching the printed value (the abstract and Discussion round it to 24%). BORDERLINE FLAGGED FOR THE ADJUDICATOR on the numerator's veracity, not on the arithmetic: the item counts sharing of UNVERIFIED information ("truth value was not known to them at the time of sharing"), so the numerator can include content that later turned out to be TRUE. That is broader than any of the schema's breadth levels; 'misleading' is coded as the broadest available. If the review requires the shared content to have been false, this row should be dropped in favour of the 31.4% row below. Sampling frame is purposive and highly unusual: self-selected subscribers to Australia's premier fact-checking newsletter, older (70% aged 60+) and highly educated (59% degree-level), 72.2% reading every issue - the authors state "we included a very specific sample and thus findings may not be generalisable to the general population." Item wording gives no recall window.

estimates.misinfo_def: Claims the respondent "later discovered were false" - falsity established retrospectively by the respondent, with no definition or external check supplied.

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-report; the respondent is the judge of the later-discovered falsity. No external verification, no fact-check linkage, no reliability statistic (single Yes/No item).
estimates.moderator_quote: Participants indicated the following: ... (v) whether they have shared claims that they later discovered were false (response options were Yes and No); and, (vi) whether they have shared possible misinformation, i.e. information for which the truth value was not known to them at the time of sharing (response options were Yes and No).
estimates.notes: definition_variant=true: same sample and same country x platform cell as the 24.3% row, but a stricter numerator (content actually discovered to be false rather than merely unverified). The two rows overlap in unknown degree and must not both enter a pool. MINOR ARITHMETIC NOTE: 440/1397 = 31.50%, while the paper prints 31.4% (Table 3 and text both say 31%/31.4%); the verbatim printed value is kept per R8. On the review's construct logic this is the cleaner 'shared misinformation' measure of the two, since falsity is asserted.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) NOT extracted - sharing of DEBUNKED information is the opposite construct (spreading corrections, not misinformation): "How frequently have you shared debunked information in the past 3 months? <5 976 (69.9%), 5-10 305 (21.8%), 10-20 75 (5.4%), >20 32 (2.3%)", summarised in the text as "approximately 30% had shared debunked information five times or more in the past 3 months". The 30% is also a cross-category sum the authors computed (21.8 + 5.4 + 2.3), and the '<5' band includes zero, so no 'any sharing' share is derivable. (2) NOT extracted - self-reported EXPOSURE exists but only as a scale mean: "Frequency of reading posts in social media that were later debunked in CoronaCheck: M = 4.58, SD = 2.96, range 1-10" (Table 4). Per the protocol, a scale mean with no share of respondents yields no row; this is the one RECALL-exposure estimate the paper could have contributed. (3) Reasons for sharing are shares of the 339 sharers, not of the sample, and describe motivation rather than prevalence: seemed interesting 121 (35.7%), second opinion 130 (38.3%), entertainment 42 (12.4%), support a cause 24 (7.1%), warn others 8 (2.4%). If the review ever codes 'within-sharer' breakdowns these are available (denominator 339). (4) NOT extracted - not misinformation measures: vaccine acceptance (~82%), newsletter engagement (16,000 subscribers, 45% open rate, 92,000 weekly ABC readership), Table 2 news-platform and motivation shares, all scale means in Table 4 (concern about fake news 8.65/10, perceived capacity to differentiate fake from genuine news 4.23/5, conspiracy mentality 5.90/11, belief in science 5.82/7), and all regression/correlation output (Tables 5-7). (5) Figures quoted from other studies (Guess et al.: 10% of 3,500 shared fake-news-site content; Irish 35% / UK 31% vaccine reluctance; Essential Research 10%->16%) are citations to elsewhere, excluded by R8. (6) Topic coded general_news, not covid19: the two sharing items sit in the generic 'Engagement with news' block with no topic restriction, even though the sample and the newsletter are COVID-19 specific - an adjudicator may reasonably prefer covid19 on framing grounds. (7) No time window is given for either sharing item ('have you ever' is implied), which makes both values non-comparable with month- or year-windowed self-report measures elsewhere in the corpus.

rob.design: Cross-sectional anonymous online survey (Qualtrics), December 2020. Frame: purposive and self-selected - a call for participants in two editions of the CoronaCheck newsletter (RMIT ABC Fact Check, ~16,000 subscribers, 45% average open rate); 1,576 Australians responded, 29 duplicates and 150 responses with >20% missing data excluded, final n = 1,397; no response rate can be computed against subscribers who saw the call. Sample is markedly unrepresentative: 40.9% aged 60-69 and 26.3% aged 70-79, 59% with a bachelor's or postgraduate degree, 72.2% read every newsletter issue, mean concern about fake news 8.65/10, belief in science significantly higher and conspiracy mentality significantly lower than in a comparison sample (Lobato et al.). Both misinformation-sharing measures are single self-reported Yes/No items with no recall window and no external verification; established scales were used for conspiracy mentality (Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire, alpha = .80 in-sample) and belief in science (Credibility of Science Scale, alpha = .89 in-sample), but these are predictors, not the prevalence measures. A priori power analysis required n = 145. Ethics approval RMIT 2020-23847-13060; data openly available on OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/2DQX7).
